intro: The most striking things the research turned up, drawn from the sources cited on each card. Relationships are given from Miles's point of view, which is the same for Jenni. For John or Hilary, an ancestor on your own side is one generation closer.

sections.title: Where the name Miles comes from

items.title: A boy who arrived in Charles Town in 1684
body: Col. Miles Brewton came to the Carolina colony with his parents on 12 July 1684, when he was about eight. He became a goldsmith, which then meant a banker, and in 1718 he was foreman of the grand jury that tried the pirate Stede Bonnet and his crew.

His granddaughter Mary Brewton married Joseph Jones. When their granddaughter Milicent Colcock was baptized in 1769, her godfather was her great-uncle Miles Brewton (1731-1775), a Charleston merchant and patriot. The name passed down through the Colcock, Ferguson and Hutson families to Miles Brewton Hutson, born in 1889, and from him to Miles.

sections.title: The Liebes family: furs, Neiman-Marcus and a tragedy

items.title: From Prussia to the Pacific fur trade
body: Herman Liebes was born in Rawicz, Prussia, in 1842 and came to New York at twenty. In October 1864 he opened a small fur workshop in San Francisco. H. Liebes & Co. grew into the leading fur house on the Pacific Coast, with stores in San Francisco and Portland, and advertised itself as the largest dealer in sealskins in the world. He died in London in 1898.

items.title: Rescued from the surf at Long Beach
body: On 2 July 1916, on a family holiday, Julien Liebes carried his thirteen-year-old son George into the surf at Long Beach. A rip tide pulled them both under while his wife Sophie and younger son Martin watched from the beach. A lifeguard pulled George out unconscious and revived him. Julien, 45, could not be saved.
George grew up to be Joan's father. Had the lifeguard not reached him, this half of the family would not exist.

items.title: Neiman-Marcus's fur buyer
body: George Julien Liebes carried the family trade to Dallas. In 1950 the census lists him as a fur director, and in 1955 Neiman-Marcus elected him a vice president. In May 1966 he paid $1,100 a skin for 40 Black Willow mink at the Hudson's Bay auction, for an $80,000 coat. Stanley Marcus reportedly whistled at the price, wished him luck, and came to New York the next day just to see the skins.

items.title: Joan: Portland, San Francisco, Dallas
body: Joan Liebes was born in Portland, Oregon, in 1931, most likely because her father was working at the family's Portland fur store. She spent her early childhood in San Francisco and moved to Dallas at eleven. She earned degrees from SMU and Stanford (Class of 1951), taught school, and later worked in personnel and training at Neiman Marcus, where her father had been an executive.

items.title: An actor who became a Charleston minister
body: The Hutson line starts with Rev. William Hutson, born in England in 1720. He began studying law, gave it up, and sailed to America in 1740 as an actor. The preacher George Whitefield converted him in New York, and he went on to lead Charleston's Circular Church. He is buried behind it.

items.title: A signer of the Articles of Confederation
body: William's son Richard Hutson, brother of Miles's direct ancestor Thomas, sat in the Continental Congress and signed the Articles of Confederation, the country's first constitution. The British captured him at the fall of Charleston in 1780 and held him at St. Augustine. He was later lieutenant governor of South Carolina and the first intendant (mayor) of Charleston. Thomas served as a militia officer in the Revolution and voted to ratify the U.S. Constitution in 1788.

items.title: The first English settler of South Carolina
body: Dr. Henry Woodward, born about 1646, is usually called the first English settler of South Carolina. When an English expedition left Port Royal in 1666, he stayed behind to live among the Native people and learn their languages. He then served the first colony as interpreter. His granddaughter Mary Woodward married Rev. William Hutson in 1743.

items.title: Kin of the Swamp Fox
body: Hester Marion, wife of Henry Gignilliat, was an aunt of Gen. Francis Marion, the Revolutionary guerrilla leader known as the Swamp Fox. Her parents were French Protestant refugees from Poitou. Her granddaughter's husband, Thomas Hutson, later served in the militia under Marion.

items.title: Huguenots from Sedan
body: Several lines go back to French Protestants (Huguenots) of Sedan, whose church registers reach the late 1500s. After Louis XIV outlawed their faith in 1685, Jacob Michaux fled to Amsterdam, where his son Abraham married Susanne Rochet in 1692. They moved to London in 1701 and by 1705 were at the Huguenot settlement of Manakin Towne, Virginia.

Family tradition says Susanne escaped France hidden in a cask. That story is handed down, not documented. The earliest ancestor named in these records is Thomas Rochet, a brewer of Sedan who died before 1638.

items.title: In Virginia by the 1660s
body: The Lockett line begins with Thomas Lockett I, a planter in Henrico County, Virginia, by 1667, who died in 1686. His wife Margaret is said to descend from Capt. Thomas Osborne, who came to Virginia on the Bona Nova in 1619. That Osborne link rests on family tradition and is marked tentative.
items.caution: The Osborne generations are the compiler's reconstruction, not a proven line.

items.title: Soldier, professor, painter
body: Charles Woodward Hutson graduated from South Carolina College in 1860 with the medal for the senior essay. He was wounded at First Manassas and captured at Seven Pines. After the war he taught Greek at LSU, modern languages at the University of Mississippi and history at Texas A&M, wrote novels, and late in life became known as a painter in New Orleans. He also edited several collections of Lafcadio Hearn's writing. His papers are held at UNC Chapel Hill.

items.title: Engineers and scientists, men and women
body: Neil Hutson earned a master's in electrical engineering from Tulane at twenty, installed radar on aircraft carriers at the end of World War II, founded the Hutson Corporation in 1964 and invented the world's smallest pistol scope. His father Miles Brewton Hutson was an electrical engineer.

The women were scientists too. His mother Adela Nelson graduated from Newcomb College in 1912 and became a chemistry teaching fellow in 1913. His sister Mary Jane made Phi Beta Kappa with a biology degree, and his aunts Sophie and Mary Hutson both completed the full civil engineering course at Texas A&M.

items.title: The same ancestors, twice
body: Napoleon Lockett married his first cousin Mary Lockett. Both were grandchildren of Stephen Lockett and Mary Clay, so those two appear twice in Miles's tree. Mary Clay's brother was Gen. Green Clay of Kentucky, father of the abolitionist Cassius Marcellus Clay.

items.title: Two lines, one Charleston church
body: Job Palmer arrived in Charleston in 1772 and served as clerk and sexton of the Circular Church for 39 years, the same church Rev. William Hutson had led a generation earlier. In 1836 Job's granddaughter Sophronia Palmer married William Ferguson Hutson. Her brother was Rev. Benjamin Morgan Palmer, the well-known pastor of First Presbyterian Church in New Orleans.

items.title: Planters, slavery and secession
body: Many of the colonial Virginia and South Carolina ancestors were planters whose wealth came from enslaved people. Their wills name them: Henry Clay's will left his granddaughter Mary Clay, later Mary Lockett, a girl named Phoebe. William Ferguson Hutson helped report and then signed South Carolina's 1860 Ordinance of Secession, and his father Richard Woodward Hutson's plantation house was burned as Sherman's army approached in 1865.
These records are part of the family history too. The people named in them, such as Phoebe, are the start of other families' histories.
